headline: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
body:
Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services

Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

headline: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
body:
Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years

New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

headline: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
body:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

headline: These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
body:
Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated

The livestream begins.

A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

headline: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
body:
Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday

A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

headline: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
body:
Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw

This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.

The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.

Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.

"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."

The 21m tree has been nicknamed Jolly Cheery

Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."

Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.

headline: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
body:
The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
body:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.

"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."

The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.

headline: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
body:
Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

headline: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
body:
Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

headline: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
body:
Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

headline: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
body:
Watch: Drone footage shows aftermath of deadly fire at Indonesian factory

At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

headline: Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
body:
Australia's Chris Bowen sits at the top table at the summit surrounded by other delegates

Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".

"That is the reality," he said on Monday.

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

headline: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
body:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep

Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".

headline: US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
body:
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.

In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.

Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.

The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.

The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.

Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.

Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.

“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”

Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption, “My Friend”.

headline: Israeli attacks on medics in occupied West Bank surge by 350%: Rights group
body:
Palestinian healthcare staff in the occupied West Bank are increasingly coming under attack from Israeli soldiers and settlers, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI).

A report released on Monday documented a 350-percent surge in incidents involving Palestinian healthcare workers between 2022 and 2024, noting that emergency responses increasingly face assault, threats and intimidation from Israeli soldiers and settlers – even when clearly identifiable as medical staff.

As part of the report, 25 medics were interviewed, and one paramedic from the Nablus area described how Israeli soldiers prevented him from reaching a wounded man.

“I was standing close to the wounded man. I could have reached him easily, but the soldiers stopped me. He lay there bleeding until he died. Only then did they leave, and we were able to reach him,” he said.

Interviewees described physical assaults, threats at gunpoint, verbal abuse and humiliating searches. All of them said they were on edge, worried that they could be stopped, attacked or prevented from reaching patients.

“Every phone call means taking a risk. And every time I leave home, there’s a chance I won’t come back,” an ambulance driver said.

The PHRI report also documented cases where medics were forced to continue treating patients while facing threats and violence themselves.

The report author, Imran Anati, said there had been a “dangerous escalation” since October 7, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started.

headline: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
body:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

headline: Unemployment to surpass 5% and ‘things will get a bit harder’, treasurer Jim Chalmers warns
body:
Economists flag rising recession risk as government forecasts economy will grow by less than 2% in 2027 and 2028

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harder before they get easier”, revealing next month’s budget update will show unemployment climbing above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years.

As economists flagged rising recessionary risks, the treasurer used a ministerial statement during question time to reveal what he described as “concerning” economic numbers in the upcoming mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

Alongside higher unemployment, high fuel costs meant inflation would slow from 4.7% now to only “the mid-3s” by the middle of next year – or about 1 percentage point higher than anticipated in the May budget.

The economy was now expected to grow by less than 2% in both 2027 and 2028.

“We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier,” Chalmers told parliament.

“If Treasury was updating the mid-year forecasts today, they would reflect this difficult environment we’re in. In the near term, they’d forecast softer growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment.”

With a majority of Australians blaming public spending for driving this year’s inflation outbreak, Chalmers promised that the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include “net savings” to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures.

headline: Burnham not ‘backtracking’ on creating closer links with EU, officials say
body:
Government wants to let trade deal ‘breathe a bit’, insiders say, after speculation No 10 is dialling back ambitions

Andy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even closer links with the EU in the wake of a landmark summit in Brussels, the Guardian has been told, after signs of an apparent slowdown in the timetable.

The prime minister has promised to set out options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, including the possibility of rejoining, saying last week that these would be outlined later in the year.

But speaking at Friday’s UK-EU summit after finalising a deal on reducing food and drink checks, emissions trading and a mutual youth mobility scheme, Burnham talked instead about “brainstorming” ideas with the EU for what comes next, with a timetable given of some months.

The apparent slowdown prompted speculation No 10 wants to dial back the political pressure and prevent his agenda being swamped by arguments about the EU, with campaign groups being formed before a possible debate about rejoining.

But after Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, talked warmly on Sunday about the benefits of more integration, government officials said this was still the aim after a “really positive” summit in which the EU side, they said, promised to be as helpful as possible with whatever comes next.

“There is no backtracking or pumping the brakes,” one said. “The government just wants to let this deal breathe a bit, and point to the benefits.”

headline: At least 24 killed and dozens missing in confectionery factory fire in Indonesia
body:
Rescuers brave unstable structures in search for missing as DNA needed to identify victims

Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore ⁠through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for ⁠about 30 people ⁠still missing.

Authorities ​were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.

Said Iqbal, ⁠a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died. He said the ​implementation of safety protocols was being ‌assessed and that he ‌would summon the factory’s chief executive.

Preliminary reports indicated the fire might have ‌been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added. The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the national police’s victim identification division.

She said body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.

The blaze had largely been contained on Sunday but firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations on Monday before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.

headline: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
body:
Choi Kyo-jin says he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams following last-minute scramble to tighten measures

South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountancy exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam, known as the suneung.

The cheat’s confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the university entrance exams, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.

The unprecedented crackdown included doubling the number of supervisors and sending emergency alerts to detect any smartphones illegally smuggled into the exam centres.

Students were also told to turn up with pencils only. Erasers were provided by the test centres, as authorities tried to reduce the chances of concealed digital devices disguised as stationery.

In addition, exam-takers were asked to avoid wearing clothes with buttons. Those who failed to comply were told they would have stickers placed over the buttons to prevent the use of hidden cameras.

The government promised a reward of at least $75,000 (£57,300) for anyone reporting cheating or misconduct, with reduced penalties for those who turned in their accomplices.

But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.

headline: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
body:
Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures

Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on ⁠Sunday night at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.

The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.

The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.

Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.

After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.

headline: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
body:
Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’

Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.

Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.

Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”

He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”

headline: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
body:
Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.

For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.

headline: Doula thought self-described birth keeper was clinically trained before NSW baby death, inquest hears
body:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears doula urged client to attend birth centre

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A doula who supported a free birth without any medical professionals present has told an inquest that she thought a self-described birth keeper who was assisting her was clinically trained.

The child, known in court as Baby R, died after the free birth. Baby R’s death is one of four being examined in a joint coronial inquest in Lismore, which has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024.

Sita Tara Kali, a doula who was expected to give evidence later on Monday, was involved in the care of two of the four babies – including Baby R, who is thought to have died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth.

On Monday morning, another doula present for Baby R’s birth, Ione Maslin, gave evidence at the inquest.

Maslin told the inquest that she was not medically trained, and had attended about 30 to 40 births before Baby R’s death. She said that Baby R’s birth was the first she had attended without a midwife present.

headline: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
body:
New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

In the 1840s, Cuba was the most important foreign source of copper ore for the UK. Copper was critical to Manchester’s cotton industry, railways and telegraphy.

Previous research has revealed that dozens of financiers involved in the founding in 1694 of the Bank of England invested in enslavement.

Now, Evans’s research reveals that ties between key figures in the UK’s financial system and enslavement of African peoples continued even after the government outlawed it.

Britain abolished its trade in enslaved people in 1807 and passed legislation abolishing slavery in most of its empire in 1833.

However, as Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act was coming into force, “City of London figures” were developing mining of El Cobre’s copper ore deposits, an operation which depended on enslavement in Spanish-controlled Cuba.

Key players in the highly lucrative operation included the Bank of England directors Charles Pascoe Grenfell (1790-1867) and William Thompson (1792-1854), acting in a private capacity.

headline: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
body:
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.

However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.

“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

headline: Manchester’s Co-op Live arena evacuated after ‘unknown substance’ released in crowd at Don Toliver concert
body:
Greater Manchester police declared a major incident on Sunday following reports of concertgoers reporting eye and respiratory symptoms

One person has been taken to hospital after an “unknown substance” was let off in the crowd during a Don Toliver concert at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena, officials said.

Greater Manchester police said a major incident was declared shortly after 10pm on Sunday following reports of people in the crowd at the US rapper’s show suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be teargas.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.

In a statement issued shortly after 2am on Monday, police said concertgoers had been safely evacuated, with several people being assessed on site for side effects.

The North West ambulance service said more than 50 people had been assessed by clinicians, with some reporting “eye and respiratory symptoms”.

“Decontamination is being carried out as a precaution and one patient has been taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment,” it said in a statement.

“We deployed several emergency crews, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene.

“Anyone at tonight’s event who has since noticed side-effects or become ill should seek medical advice.”

Greater Manchester police assistant chief constable Steph Parker said more than 12,000 people had been safely evacuated from the arena.

headline: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts
body:
Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally

Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Twenty-seven of those trusts are in such dire financial straits that they have rated lack of money as the biggest threat they face. Six have given that danger a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. A much-larger number of trusts have launched cost-cutting programmes to save as much as £106m each this year by limiting the services they provide and shrinking their workforces, despite understaffing being widespread across the NHS.

The six include King’s College hospital NHS trust in London, which is seeking to save £85m this year, and the St George’s, Epsom and St Helier hospital group, also in the capital, which has a savings target of £91m. The others are the North Midlands, Gloucestershire, and Doncaster and Bassetlaw acute trusts, and Birmingham and Solihull mental health trust.

headline: Alleged Mexican drug cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’ arrested in special forces raid
body:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.

His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.

Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.

The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.

headline: Rally rush brings city to a standstill
body:
Multiple rallies and protest sit-ins trigger traffic diversions across Karachi

Karachi's major arteries descended into traffic chaos on Sunday as multiple political and religious rallies brought traffic to a grinding halt, leaving hundreds of motorists stranded, commuters fuming and routine movement across major parts of the metropolis severely disrupted. With police barricading key arteries and diverting vehicles onto already congested alternative routes, many citizens faced prolonged delays before the city's traffic network gradually returned to normal following the conclusion of the demonstrations.

A series of political and religious rallies brought large parts of Karachi's road network to a crawl on Sunday, leaving hundreds of vehicles stranded and commuters struggling to reach their destinations as police blocked key arteries and diverted traffic onto alternative routes. Normal traffic flow was restored across all major thoroughfares after the demonstrations and rallies ended.

A rally organised by Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, with participants arriving from different parts of the city, converged at Drig Road, prompting police to erect barricades and close one track of Sharae Faisal to traffic. The restrictions triggered a severe traffic jam around Drig Road, with hundreds of vehicles caught in the congestion. The road connecting Millennium Mall to Drig Road was also closed.

headline: No urgent case for rupee depreciation
body:
Current-account gap, remittances and reserves are the numbers to watch

A shopkeeper in Larkana may have little reason to follow Pakistan's debt-to-GDP ratio or the State Bank of Pakistan's (SBP) weekly reserves statement. Ask him what the dollar is trading at, however, and he may be able to tell you before he checks his phone. A weaker rupee raises the cost of replacing the imported goods on his shelves. For the family next door receiving money from Dubai, the same dollar buys more rupees. Few economic indicators travel as far, or mean such different things to the people watching them.

Nor do many indicators attract as many forecasts. The rupee's last sharp fall is still fresh in public memory. From around Rs160, the dollar climbed to Rs307.10 in the interbank market on September 5, 2023. The distinction matters. The dollar became about 92% more expensive, while the rupee lost roughly 48% of its dollar value. Some 38 months later, in the third week of November 2026, the dollar was trading near Rs276.5. Does the passage of three years make another sharp adjustment overdue?

headline: States agree to UN talks aiming to regulate 'killer robots' by 2028
body:
Around 100 nations backed the move, but US, Russia and Israel opposed binding measures

UN talks on regulating weapons with little or no human oversight ended on Saturday with a pledge for further discussions to develop new rules within two years, an outcome weakened by Russia's opposition and disappointing human ​rights groups.

Proponents had called for legally binding rules within a short timeframe to regulate weapons ​systems that can identify and engage targets with varying degrees of autonomy, ⁠sometimes called "killer robots".

Around 100 countries backed this position, but big arms-producing nations like the US, Russia ​and Israel opposed this, resulting in a watered-down agreement that left open the question of whether ​future measures would be legally binding.

The member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons had been meeting in Geneva since Monday as alarm grows over the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems in conflicts, including in Ukraine, ​Sudan and the Middle East.

The UN secretary-general, the pope and the Red Cross have all called ​for strict and legally binding rules.

The meeting's Swiss chair, Julien Thoeni, hailed the deal as a significant achievement for ‌humanitarian ⁠disarmament after more than 10 years of talks.

Read More: Saudi Arabia says it intercepts three Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh

“It shows that even in today’s deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results," he told reporters in a hoarse voice as talks concluded after 4am (0300 GMT).

headline: NDMA issues nationwide alert ahead of pre-monsoon rains, warns of hazards
body:
Says intermittent pre-monsoon rains expected from June 28 to July 3

National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) on Sunday advised citizens to stay alert as intermittent pre-monsoon rains were expected across Pakistan from June 28 to July 3.

According to NDMA officials talking to media channels, a dangerous combination of intense heat and expected pre-monsoon rainfall was likely to accelerate glacier melting, triggering a sharp rise in water levels in rivers and streams across Gilgit-Baltistan (G-B), Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), and Azad Jammu and Kashmir.

The authority warned that vulnerable mountainous regions face heightened risks of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), flash floods, and landslides during the forecast period due to rapidly changing and unstable weather conditions.

NDMA issues strong countrywide alert ahead of pre-monsoon rainfall spell, warns of hazards pic.twitter.com/JuCxbEGIZu

Residents, tourists and travellers have been strongly advised to exercise extreme caution in high-risk districts, including Hunza, Nagar, Ghizer, Skardu, Shigar, Ghanche, Kharmang, Astore, Diamer, Upper and Lower Chitral and Swat, where sudden weather shifts could create life-threatening situations.

NDMA further urged the public to strictly avoid unnecessary movement near rivers, streams, glacial lakes and riverbanks, stressing the importance of immediate reporting of any unusual or hazardous conditions to local authorities to prevent loss of life and property.

Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs) have been placed on high alert with strict instructions to ensure full emergency preparedness, rapid response capability and coordinated action in case of any disaster triggered by the expected weather system.

headline: Taliban feel weight of Pakistan's pressure
body:
Kabul likely to take steps to address concerns

Pakistan will persist with its current Afghan strategy, believing that sustained pressure is beginning to weigh heavily on the Taliban regime, with recent developments suggesting that Kabul may be taking some steps to address Islamabad's concerns, even if their effectiveness remains uncertain.

Sources familiar with the developments told The Express Tribune on Sunday that reports suggesting a possible engagement between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban in Doha were incorrect. There has been no such engagement, they said, adding that Islamabad has no immediate plans to change its approach.

Pakistan will continue with its current policy until the Taliban regime takes clear and verifiable action against the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist outfits, the sources maintained.

They, however, acknowledged that the Taliban had recently taken certain steps that could indicate a willingness to respond to Pakistan's concerns. They confirmed that the Taliban authorities had detained some TTP terrorists, although the circumstances and nature of their detention remained unclear.

While describing these moves as potentially cosmetic, the sources said they could nevertheless be an indication that Pakistan's sustained pressure was beginning to produce some results. "At this stage, we are not sure whether these detentions are permanent or just an eyewash," one source said.

"What we want is for the Taliban regime to take the same action against the TTP as it usually takes against its other opponents," the source added.

headline: Pakistan, Oman seal $200m energy deal
body:
Two sides agree to establish a regular commercial framework for supplying petroleum products to PSO

Pakistan and Oman have signed an agreement to strengthen petroleum trade, with Oman's OQ Trading extending a $200 million credit facility to Pakistan State Oil (PSO) for the purchase of petroleum products.

Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik and Oman's Minister of Energy and Minerals, Engineer Salim Al Aufi, attended the signing ceremony in Muscat, where the two sides agreed to establish a regular commercial framework for supplying petroleum products to PSO.

The agreement is being viewed as an important step towards strengthening Pakistan's energy security and diversifying its sources of petroleum imports, as the Strait of Hormuz continues to be choked by the US-Iran conflict into its ninth month.

During their meeting, the two ministers also agreed to expand bilateral cooperation in the oil, gas and minerals sectors. They welcomed the establishment of a joint working group between the two countries in the oil and gas sector and agreed to use the forum to advance cooperation in energy and minerals.

OQ Trading supplied more than one million metric tonnes of petrol to PSO in 2026, while its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplies to Pakistan are expected to exceed 120,000 metric tonnes by the end of the year. Both countries also expressed their commitment to exploring new opportunities for trade partnerships and investment in the energy sector.

headline: Trump says US to penalize firms building data centers abroad
body:
Data centres power AI systems, and a proposed tax could disrupt global expansion by US developers

President Donald Trump said on Friday ​that the US would penalize American companies that build data ‌centers overseas, a move he said is intended to help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with its Chinese counterparts.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data ​centers outside of our country," Trump said while discussing AI at ​a White House news conference following his trip to Asia. ⁠He said he would impose a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data ​centers abroad.

Read More: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers

Data centers are critical to the AI boom because they provide ​the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex AI systems, and a penalty could complicate the global AI buildout. Several major American data center developers build and ​operate such facilities outside the US, including Equinix and Digital Realty.

Data center ​developers often locate facilities close to users to reduce delays for time-sensitive tasks such as ‌payment ⁠processing. Transmitting large volumes of data over long distances can also add significant costs.

Trump has been a staunch advocate for data center construction in the US, a position that is unpopular with voters. Data centers have drawn opposition ​in communities nationwide over ​concerns about electricity ⁠demand, utility costs and other local impacts.

headline: We have to keep Netanyahu 'a little bit sane', says Trump
body:
US President Donald Trump delivered a blunt critique of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a press interview, stating their relationship is "good, but we have to keep him a little bit sane"

The remark came when Trump was asked by Axious, an American media outlet, about his ties with the Israeli premier amid ongoing efforts to end fighting in Lebanon.

Trump asserted he can control Israeli military actions in Lebanon because officials there "do as I say."

He highlighted American military superiority, saying that the US provides "the guns" and "B-2 bombers," and claimed that without his intervention, Israel would have been "eviscerated," echoing his remarks earlier this week asserting: "Without the United States, there would be no Israel."

Earlier this week, the US president said he advised Netanyahu to use a "softer touch" in Leb-anon, saying Israel does not have to "knock down a building every time somebody walks into it that's from Hezbollah," referring to frequent Israeli bombing of Lebanon, including many residential areas.

headline: AI schooling hinges on teacher training
body:
Workshops for 25,898 focal persons across Punjab begin today

The Punjab education authorities are preparing to introduce artificial intelligence (AI) in thousands of government schools through a training programme for 25,898 nominated teachers amid questions about digital facilities and ability of the institutions to sustain technology-based teaching after the workshops.

The provincial school education department is scheduled to begin the programme on Monday in collaboration with the Punjab Education Curriculum, Training and Assessment Authority (PECTAA).

According to the PECTAA, the teachers' training will be organised at the tehsil level in five batches.

One teacher from each government primary and elementary school will be nominated as an AI focal person, for which the district chief executive officers of education have been instructed to complete nominations and ensure attendance.

The first batch of workshops is scheduled for November 23 and 24, followed by subsequent training sessions by December 3.

The participants have been directed to bring a laptop, smartphone or school tablet to take part in practical activities.

The training will cover AI-assisted lesson planning, student assessments, development of educational material and use of the technology to address individual learning requirements. Safe, ethical and responsible use of AI in classrooms will also form part of the programme.

The trained focal persons will assist colleagues in their schools in completing the training course and adopting AI-supported teaching methods.

The nominated teachers will require time, resources and institutional support to guide their colleagues alongside their regular teaching responsibilities.

headline: Bangladesh ex-PM loses right to appeal
body:
Bangladesh's former premier Sheikh Hasina can no longer appeal her death sentence after the 30-day deadline for filing an appeal expired, the chief prosecutor said on Monday.

"Those sentenced to death by the court, including Sheikh Hasina, who have not appealed within 30 days of the verdict, will no longer have the opportunity to do so," Md Aminul Islam told reporters.

Last November, Hasina was sentenced to death by the Dhaka-based International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity and for her role in a brutal crackdown during the 2024 uprising that ousted her government.

At least 1,400 people were killed and thousands were injured in the uprising by Hasina's security forces and supporters of her Awami League party, according to the UN.

"Now, what is left is the execution of the verdict," said the prosecutor.

However, he said, the "government has the absolute inherent power to suspend or cancel any punishment".

She is in self-imposed exile, living in India after fleeing the country.

headline: Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy 'evidence'
body:
Albanese says Palestinians should take charge of clearance

A UN expert said on Monday that Israeli clearance of rubble in Gaza could destroy valuable evidence of "atrocity crimes" and prevent the recovery of human remains.

Israel's assault on Gaza - started after the deadly raid into Israel by Hamas in October 2023 - has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United Nations.

Francesca Albanese, the UN expert on the Palestinian territories, said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified before full clearance started.

She issued a statement headlined: "UN expert warns Israeli rubble-clearing could erase traces of atrocity crimes" and said Palestinians should be behind any plans to remove waste.

"In devastated Gaza, rubble is not just construction waste. It is part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years," she said.

She said that multiple sources had confirmed Israeli companies were involved in the clearance, without naming those sources. Her office did not immediately respond to questions on where that information had come from.

Israel's Foreign Ministry, its Prime Minister's Office and military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, all have fiercely disagreed with Albanese, who has emerged as one of the most vocal critics of Israel's military actions in Gaza.

headline: Murals turn Arts Council into canvas for global voices
body:
Turning concrete walls into canvases for peace, friendship and environmental consciousness, international artists have added a new splash of colour to the Arts Council of Pakistan Karachi, as the 24th day of the World Culture Festival 2026 celebrated the power of art to transcend borders.

Two murals, including an anti-war artwork by Colombian artist Jhon Ramirez and Concrete Horizon by Italian muralist Edoardo Ettore, were formally inaugurated on the exterior walls of the Arts Council building, drawing attention to the festival's growing emphasis on cultural diplomacy.

The anti-war mural was unveiled by Arts Council President Muhammad Ahmed Shah, Canadian Deputy High Commissioner Tariq Ali and German Consul General Thomas Schultze, while Ettore's artwork was jointly inaugurated by Shah, Italian Consul General Fabrizio Bielli and the artist.

Speaking at the ceremony, Shah said culture was an effective bridge between nations, capable of bringing people closer while strengthening trade and diplomatic ties. Referring to his four decades of work in cultural engagement, he said the Arts Council was striving to project Pakistan's positive image through culture and diplomacy.

Appreciating the contribution of international artists, he said they had produced remarkable work while the Arts Council had provided them with a platform to showcase their creativity. He said three editions of the World Culture Festival had been organised over the past two years, transforming Karachi into an increasingly important international cultural hub.

headline: Brilliant Verstappen wins Las Vegas Grand Prix
body:
The Red Bull driver beat Norris by just 0.6 seconds

Red Bull driver Max Verstappen roared to a superb victory at the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday, holding his nerve in a thrilling 50-lap battle to claim the 75th win of his career.

Verstappen dug deep to fend off Mercedes' newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli and teammate George Russell in a race that saw a jaw-dropping 35 lead changes.

McLaren's Lando Norris took second place while Oscar Piastri finished third at the end of a hectic final few laps which saw Russell strike a wall before Antonelli faded down the stretch.

"Crazy, I mean really, really surreal -- something that I've never seen before in Formula One myself," Verstappen said after clinching victory by six tenths of a second.

"Just a crazy amount of fighting. The slipstream was so big that it was just impossible to drive off. Crazy how many people were just following. "So yeah, very happy with such a crazy race to come out on top."

Verstappen's victory leaves the Dutchman second in the standings with 304 points, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton third on 267 points. Russell is fourth with 264 points, the same total as Norris.

With the drivers' championship already settled, Verstappen started on pole looking for a win to boost his chances of finishing second behind Antonelli.

headline: India, Bulgaria discuss bilateral ties, IMEC, Black Sea situation
body:
Published - November 22, 2026 05:45 am IST - New Delhi

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar shakes hands with Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova ahead of their bilateral meeting at Hyderabad House, in New Delhi on November 22, 2026. | Photo Credit: ANI

India and Bulgaria on Saturday (November 22, 2026) reviewed their bilateral cooperation in trade, security, technology and other areas, even as the two sides also held discussions on IMEC, the Black Sea situation and the Ukraine conflict.

Also read | ‘Not an era of war’: In Bulgaria, Jaishankar calls for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar held talks with his Bulgarian counterpart, Velislava Petrova, at the Hyderabad House in Delhi.

"Pleased to meet FM Bulgaria @vpetrova_mfa this afternoon. Reviewed our bilateral cooperation, including in trade, connectivity, investments, technology, security and talent mobility. Appreciated growing P2P linkages & cultural exchanges between our two countries, as well as deepening India-EU ties," Mr. Jaishankar later posted on X.

Agreed that the India-EU FTA should be followed through by "vigorous exchanges between our businesses". Also exchanged views on the prospects of IMEC (India Middle East Europe Economic Corridor) and other connectivity initiatives, he added.

"Appreciated the discussion on the Black Sea situation and the Ukraine conflict," the EAM said in his post.

headline: U.S. panel urges India dialogue for Dalai Lama succession, warns of China legitimacy contest
body:
Updated - November 23, 2026 11:36 am IST - Washington

Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama. File | Photo Credit: PTI

A U.S. Congressional panel has recommended setting up a senior-level channel with India for succession contingency planning for the 14th Dalai Lama, contending that China may turn the process into an international contest over legitimacy.

A U.S. Congressional panel has recommended establishing a senior-level channel with India for succession contingency planning for the 14th Dalai Lama, arguing that China may turn the process into an international legitimacy contest.

The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, in a report to the U.S. Congress, made a strong pitch to recognise the Gaden Phodrang Trust as the sole legitimate authority to identify and recognise the successor to the 14th Dalai Lama.

The report by the bipartisan Commission said China was likely to use coercive tools to shape the outcome of the succession process.

It said that the U.S. Congress should adopt a policy of not recognising any successor to the Dalai Lama who is selected or installed by China.

Also Read: How will the Dalai Lama’s successor be chosen? Explained

“To carry out this policy and ensure U.S. government readiness for the Dalai Lama’s succession, Congress should direct the Secretary of State to… establish a senior-level channel with the Government of India for succession contingency planning, including intelligence sharing on Chinese influence operations,” the report said.

headline: Cargo ship bound for Russia's Kaliningrad hit by drones, Finland tightens security
body:
Updated - November 21, 2026 10:21 pm IST - HELSINKI

The damaged Russian cargo ship Sparta II, in a location given as the Gulf of Finland, November 21, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

A cargo ship bound for Russia's Baltic exclave ‌of Kaliningrad was struck by drones in international waters in ​the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, Russian and Finnish authorities ⁠said, prompting Finland to tighten security measures in the area.

The vessel was damaged west of Russia's Gogland island, caught fire and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters, Finland's Defence ‌Forces said, corroborating an earlier account by Russian officials.

Leningrad region Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said the vessel had been attacked by two ‌drones in international waters about three nautical miles from Russia's border. ‌The ⁠crew was being evacuated and the extent of the damage ⁠was being assessed, he said.

Finland's Defence Ministry said the military had reintroduced temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland as a precaution to protect civilians and enable authorities ​to operate if drones needed ‌to be intercepted.

Finland had informed its allies about the incident, the ministry said.

Estonia's Police and Border Guard Board said in an emailed statement it had been informed that a fire had broken out aboard the Russian ‌cargo vessel Sparta II and that preliminary information indicated there had ​been explosions on board.

headline: India, Finland seek to deepen economic ties through startup cooperation: Envoy Mikko Kivikoski
body:
Updated - November 21, 2026 06:39 pm IST - New Delhi

Mikko Kivikoski. File | Photo Credit: The Hindu

“India and Finland are looking to deepen economic cooperation by strengthening ties between their startup ecosystems and promoting greater two-way investment,” Finnish Ambassador to India Mikko Kivikoski has said.

"We want to engage more with the Indian startup actors. And of course, at the end of the day, this is all about advancing the economic cooperation between our countries. And here we see the startup sector, startup ecosystems, as an important part of that cooperation," Mr. Kivikoski told PTI.

The Ambassador was speaking at an unconventional startup event held at the Embassy of Finland in New Delhi on Friday (November 20, 2026), where entrepreneurs stepped into an ice-cold pool to pitch their ideas, drawing on Finland's winter-swimming tradition. "We have quite a long tradition in Finland for these kinds of events," Mr. Kivikoski said.

"This year has been record-high when it comes to interaction and engagement between Finland and India," he said, referring to visits by the Finnish Prime Minister and President, as well as meetings between the leaders of the two countries.

The Ambassador said the two sides agreed to elevate their bilateral relationship to a Strategic Partnership in Digitalisation and Sustainability during Finnish President Alexander Stubb's state visit to India in March.

headline: China slams ‘malicious’ U.S. ban on telecom firms’ phone number access
body:
Updated - November 22, 2026 12:19 pm IST - BEIJING

The order by the Federal Communications Commission aims to curb access to U.S. phone numbers by “bad actors” it said were responsible for “illegal robocalling campaigns”. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Beijing's Commerce Ministry denounced on Sunday (November 22, 2026) a recent move by Washington to cut direct access for Chinese telecom giants to U.S. phone numbers, calling the decision "malicious".

The order, approved in a vote on Thursday (November 19, 2026) by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), aims to curb access to U.S. phone numbers by "bad actors" it said were responsible for "illegal robocalling campaigns".

Affected entities include China's three biggest telecom firms, the state-owned China Unicom, China Telecom and China Mobile.

"Without any factual basis, (the FCC) has violated the principles of non-discrimination and fair competition to wantonly smear and maliciously suppress Chinese telecommunications firms," Beijing's Commerce Ministry said in an online statement.

Recent moves by the FCC aimed at "decoupling" ties in the telecoms sector "run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state", it said.

They "undermine the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations", it said, urging Washington to "revoke" the steps and warning China may take its own "necessary measures".

The criticism by Beijing comes after President Xi Jinping hosted his U.S. counterpart Donald Trump at a regional summit this week in Shenzhen, where the Chinese leader hailed "stable and improved" ties with Washington.

headline: Finland detects drone attack on Russian cargo ship in Baltic
body:
Updated - November 21, 2026 07:26 pm IST - Helsinki, Finland

A photo published by the Finnish Border Guard of the damaged Russian cargo ship in a location given as the Gulf of Finland on November 21, 2026. Photo: Finnish Border Guard via Reuters.

Finland’s military detected a drone attack on Saturday morning (November 21, 2026) on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, which caused the vessel to catch fire, the Nordic country’s authorities said.

The Finnish Defence Ministry did not specify who was behind the drone strike, but Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a message on X: “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity... Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Fighting off a Russian invasion now in its fifth year, Ukraine has stepped up its long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the front lines.

“On Saturday morning, the Finnish Defence Forces detected a drone attack against a Russian cargo vessel west of Suursaari, in the eastern Gulf of Finland, in international waters,” the Ministry said in a statement.

According to Finnish border guards dispatched to the scene the ship caught fire and began drifting towards Finnish waters after the strike.

“The situation currently poses no danger to other vessels,” the border service said in a press release.

Authorities gave no immediate details of the boat’s crew.

Finland immediately informed NATO of the strike, the Defence Ministry said.

headline: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown kills 2
body:
Updated - November 21, 2026 10:08 pm IST - Kyiv

Firefighters work at the site of a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in this handout picture released on November 21, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

A Russian strike on the centre of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday (November 21, 2026).

Meanwhile, a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday (November 21, 2026) after it was hit by drones, Finnish and Russian officials said. The Finnish Prime Minister warned that the war was spilling into the region.

A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday (November 20, 2026) night on Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.

The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Mr. Vilkul said.

Video footage published by the regional branch of the Ukrainian State Emergency Service appeared to show further strikes while ambulance and firefighting crews were responding at the scene, as fires burned around them.

“First, two ballistic missiles. And then, when the emergency and rescue operation began, three more rockets hit doctors, rescuers, and utility workers,” Mr. Vilkul wrote on Telegram.

headline: Indonesia says 24 killed in factory blaze as rescuers search for dozens missing
body:
Updated - November 23, 2026 11:01 am IST - JAKARTA

In this aerial photo taken using a drone, smoke billows from the ruins of a candy factory following a fire in Serang, Banten Province, Indonesia, on November 22, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

Indonesia confirmed on Monday (November 23, 2026) the deaths of 24 people in a fire that ​tore through a factory at the weekend, as rescuers braved ‌unstable structures in the burned wreckage in the ​search for about 30 people still missing.

Authorities ⁠were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday (November 21, 2026) evening in one building of the ‌PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about an hour’s drive ‌from the capital Jakarta.

Said Iqbal, a presidential adviser ‌on ⁠labour issues, told reporters 24 people had ⁠died, adding implementation of safety protocols was being assessed and that he would summon the factory’s chief executive.
